1: # AI Academy Final Exercise — Student Guide, Part 1: Data analysis and deployment
2: 
3: Nov 2, 2026 · @Matteo Bonas
4: 
5: ## How the exercise works
6: 
7: The exercise is divided in 2 parts. This guide covers **Part 1**: analyse your dataset, then deploy an app on it. You will keep the same dataset, repository and environment across both parts, so reuse and adapt your code instead of starting over.
8: 
9: **Nothing is graded**. You finish with a *level profile*: for each skill area you are rated Emerging, Proficient, Advanced or "not yet shown". The goal of the hands-on is to help you identify the areas in which you need to strenghten your proficiency.
10: 
11: | Task | What you deliver | Timebox |
12: | --- | --- | --- |
13: | Task 1: Exploratory data analysis | Analysis code, figures, short report | 2:30–3:00 h |
14: | Task 2: App deployment | Containerised app with interactive data exploration, short report | 2:00–2:30 h |
15: 
16: Every task ends with a short Markdown report written in your own words, using the templates in the starter repository. The exercise closes with your presentation at the end of Part 2 so build Part 1 so you can show it, explain your choices and change it live then. Feel free to use notebooks, notes, [ADRs](https://cognitect.com/blog/2011/11/15/documenting-architecture-decisions) and [charts](https://mermaid.ai/live) to help you plan and to document changes.
17: 
18: ## Part 1 tasks
19: 
20: A task counts as completed when its **minimum objectives** are met tough feel fre to add and your objectives (but do not forget to document them!). Unfinished work is normal: stop and tag when the timebox ends.
21: 
22: **Task 1: Exploratory data analysis.** Load your dataset, run a statistical analysis, find and fix data issues, and present your findings.
23: 
24: - Data loading: reproducible code that fetches or reads the raw files.
25: - Statistical analysis: distributions, correlations, target behaviour, anomalies.
26: - Data wrangling: missing values, outliers, types, encodings, leakage risks; say what you fixed and why.
27: - Visualisation and presentation: labelled charts that each back a clear claim.
28: 
29: **Task 2: App deployment.** Turn your analysis into an app that runs in containers.
30: 
31: - Build an app for interactive exploration of your data (framework of your choice).
32: - Containerise it with your own Dockerfile and deploy it with Docker Compose or Kubernetes manifests on minikube.
33: 
34: **Minimum objectives:** a comprehensive statistical analysis; data issues identified and remediated where possible; critical reasoning about the dataset; findings presented clearly; an application designed, built and deployed.
35: 
36: **Advanced objectives:** interactive visualisations that convey the most important findings; the app designed and deployed as microservices.
37: 
38: ### What reviewers look at
39: 
40: | Task | Skill areas on your profile |
41: | --- | --- |
42: | Task 1 | Data quality handling, insights backed by charts, visualisation, reproducibility (runs from a fresh clone) |
43: | Task 2 | Deployment works end to end, image quality (slim, pinned, non-root), configuration (env vars, secrets handling), trade-off reasoning, documentation |

1: # Task 1 report: Exploratory data analysis
2: 
3: | Field | Value |
4: | --- | --- |
5: | Student | Stefano Negri Merlo |
6: | Dataset | Adult Census Income (`census_income.csv`) |
7: | Task | 1 |
8: | Tag / commit | `task1` |
9: | How to run | `cd part_1 && uv run python scripts/prepare_dataset.py && uv run python run.py` |
10: | Timebox | 4 h (finished) |
11: 
12: ## 1. Summary
13: 
14: I analysed the Adult Census Income dataset (48,598 rows after cleaning, 23.55% above $50K) and built a reproducible pipeline that prepares the data, trains a random forest and a neural network, and exports predictions, ROC/PR curves and confusion matrices. The random forest reaches 85.0% accuracy and 0.664 F1 at a 0.5 cut-off; the neural network reaches 0.896 ROC AUC. Two operating points were selected from the neural network's curves: the ROC point closest to the top-left corner (threshold 0.250, recall 0.829, precision 0.566) and the PR point closest to the top-right corner (threshold 0.362, precision 0.645, recall 0.739, F1 0.689). The main limitation is a single 80/20 holdout.
15: 
16: **Evidence:** `../part_1/src/task1`, `part_1/data/nn_pred.csv`, `part_1/data/nn_roc.csv`, `part_1/data/nn_prc.csv`.
17: 
18: ## 2. Goal and success criteria
19: 
20: **Goal.** Task 1 asks for a reproducible analysis of the chosen dataset: load the raw file, describe distributions and target behaviour, find and fix data-quality problems, and present each finding with a labelled chart. I extended the analysis with two predictive baselines (random forest and neural network) and with threshold selection on the neural network's ROC and precision-recall curves, so that the cleaned dataset and the evaluation protocol can be reused in Task 2.
21: 
22: | Criterion | How it is measured | Target | Result |
23: | --- | --- | --- | --- |
24: | Reproducible pipeline | Re-run the two commands at the top from the repository root | Predictions and all five plots are regenerated | Passed; rerun completed and reproduced the same metrics |
25: | Data-quality problems identified and fixed | Row counts, null counts, duplicate and category checks | Every detected issue either fixed or documented | 244 invalid rows removed; duplicate `education-num` dropped after a 1:1 check; 29 duplicates and 2,794–2,804 `?` values documented |
26: | Two models compared on the same holdout | Accuracy, precision, recall, F1, ROC AUC | Both models above the 76.19% majority-class baseline | RF 85.01%; NN 84.10% at the PR threshold; NN AUC 0.896 |
27: | Two NN operating points selected from the curves | Explicit criterion in `roc_prc.py` | One ROC point and one PR point with reported metrics | Thresholds 0.250 and 0.362 |
28: | Labelled figures | Visual inspection and captions with values | Every figure states a claim and a number | Five figures in `part_1/plots` |
29: 
30: **Evidence:** regenerated `part_1/data/*.csv` and `part_1/plots/*.png`; metrics recomputed from the saved predictions with scikit-learn.
31: 
32: ## 3. Approach and key decisions
33: 
34: **Main findings.** The target is imbalanced: 11,443 of 48,598 rows are above $50K (23.55%), so predicting the majority class already gives 76.19% accuracy. Income rises sharply with education (Prof-school 71.7%, Doctorate 71.5%, Masters 54.4%, Bachelors 40.8%, HS-grad 15.7%), is much more frequent among married-civil-spouse people (44.1%) than never-married people (4.4%), and among men (29.9%) than women (10.7%). People above $50K are older (44.2 vs 36.9 years), work more hours (45.3 vs 38.8 per week) and more often have a non-zero capital gain (19.6% vs 4.2%). A random forest fitted on all features ranks age (0.236), hours-per-week (0.117), capital-gain (0.101), married-civ-spouse (0.078) and relationship-husband (0.044) as the strongest predictors; `fnlwgt` has essentially no linear relation with the target (correlation −0.006).
35: 
36: | # | Finding | Decision | Alternative considered | Where in the code |
37: | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
38: | D1 | 244 rows (0.50%) have `capital-gain = 99999`, a sentinel value rather than a real gain; the next largest value is 41,310 | Remove those rows | Impute the gain, cap it, or keep it as an outlier | `part_1/scripts/prepare_dataset.py`, line 17 |
39: | D2 | `fnlwgt` is a census sampling weight, not a personal attribute, and is uncorrelated with the target | Drop the column | Keep and scale it, or use it as a sample weight | `part_1/scripts/prepare_dataset.py`, lines 24–27 |
40: | D3 | `education-num` and `education` encode the same 16 levels; the mapping is exactly one-to-one in both directions | Drop `education-num`, keep the more interpretable `education` | Keep the ordinal form, or keep both | `part_1/scripts/prepare_dataset.py`; check in `../part_1/src/task1` |
41: | D4 | The raw income column has four spellings (`>50K`, `>50K.`, `<=50K`, `<=50K.`) caused by a trailing period | Normalise to a boolean target with `isin([">50K", ">50K."])` | Label encoding without normalisation, which would create four classes | `part_1/scripts/prepare_dataset.py`, line 49 |
42: | D5 | Eight categorical columns have no natural order, and three contain a `?` placeholder (workclass 5.75%, occupation 5.77%, native-country 1.74%) | One-hot encode all eight columns and keep `?` as its own category | Impute or drop the `?` rows, or use target encoding | `part_1/scripts/prepare_dataset.py`, lines 31–45; yields 106 features |
43: | D6 | The numeric features are on different scales and capital gain/loss are heavily zero-inflated (median 0, max 41,310) | Trees consume the raw values; the neural network gets a `StandardScaler` inside its pipeline | Quantile or log transforms for every model | `../part_1/src/task1`, lines 14–20 |
44: | D7 | A single model family could hide model-specific behaviour | Compare a random forest (100 trees) with a neural network on the same split | Logistic regression or gradient boosting as the only baseline | `../part_1/src/task1` |
45: | D8 | Threshold choice matters more than the ranking itself when the positive class is 23.55% | Train the NN with `MLPRegressor` to obtain a continuous score, then choose the cut-off from the curves | `MLPClassifier` with `predict_proba` and a fixed 0.5 cut-off | `../part_1/src/task1`, lines 14–20; `../part_1/src/task1` |
46: | D9 | The ROC and PR curves have different goals: the ROC balances both classes, the PR focuses on the positive class | Select the ROC point closest to (0,1) and the PR point closest to (1,1) | Fixed 0.5, maximum F1, or Youden's J | `../part_1/src/task1`, `best_point`; used in `main.py`, lines 66–67 |
47: | D10 | A single holdout is fast but noisy | Use an 80/20 split with `random_state=42` so the comparison is repeatable | k-fold cross-validation or nested CV | `../part_1/src/task1`, line 31 |
48: | D11 | Figures and metrics must be reproducible without a notebook | Persist predictions and curves as CSV and plots as PNG | Keep results only in a notebook | `../part_1/src/task1`, lines 41–50 and 60–111 |
49: 
50: **Pipeline:** raw CSV → drop 99999 gains → drop `fnlwgt` and `education-num` → one-hot encode 8 categoricals → boolean target → random-forest feature ranking → 80/20 split → RF and NN → predictions to CSV → ROC/PR and confusion matrices.
51: 
52: **Evidence:** `part_1/scripts/prepare_dataset.py`, `../part_1/src/task1`; statistics recomputed on `datasets/census_income.csv`.
53: 
54: ## 4. Results
55: 
56: | Result | Value | Baseline or reference |
57: | --- | --- | --- |
58: | Rows after cleaning / positive rate | 48,598 / 23.55% | 48,842 raw rows / 23.93% before removing invalid gains |
59: | Majority-class accuracy | 76.19% | Always predict `<=50K` |
60: | RF accuracy / precision / recall / F1 | 85.01% / 71.16% / 62.27% / 0.664 | Majority class; 0.5 cut-off |
61: | RF balanced accuracy | 0.772 | 0.500 random |
62: | NN ROC AUC | 0.896 | 0.500 random |
63: | NN at ROC threshold 0.250: accuracy / precision / recall / F1 | 80.81% / 56.63% / 82.89% / 0.673 | Majority class; 0.5 cut-off (F1 0.658) |
64: | NN at PR threshold 0.362: accuracy / precision / recall / F1 | 84.10% / 64.54% / 73.85% / 0.689 | Majority class; all-positive F1 0.381 |
65: | NN balanced accuracy at PR threshold | 0.806 | 0.500 random |
66: 
67: The RF row uses hard 0/1 predictions, so its "AUC" would be a balanced-accuracy value (0.772), not a probability AUC. The NN has a genuine continuous score because it is a regressor. The RF is more precise at 0.5 (71.2% vs 64.5%) but the NN at the PR threshold has higher recall (73.9% vs 62.3%) and a higher F1 (0.689 vs 0.664). The ROC threshold is the high-recall option (82.9% recall, 1,469 false positives); the PR threshold trades 530 fewer false positives for 210 more false negatives.

91: ## 5. Problems and how you handled them
92: 
93: | Problem | Cause | What you did | Status |
94: | --- | --- | --- | --- |
95: | 244 rows with `capital-gain = 99999` | The value is a missing-value sentinel, not a real capital gain | Removed the rows (0.50% of the data) | Solved |
96: | `education-num` duplicated `education` | The two columns are two encodings of the same 16 levels | Verified the one-to-one mapping with `check_one_to_one_correspondence`, then dropped `education-num` | Solved |
97: | Four income labels instead of two | Trailing periods in the source file | Normalised to a boolean target | Solved |
98: | Class imbalance (23.55% positive) | The dataset over-represents `<=50K` | Reported precision/recall/F1 besides accuracy and selected thresholds; no resampling or class weights | Workaround |
99: | 2,794–2,804 `?` values in workclass/occupation and 847 in native-country | The source uses `?` instead of an empty field | Kept `?` as its own one-hot category so no rows were lost | Workaround |
100: | The RF probabilities were not saved | `random_forest_predict` returns `rf.predict`, i.e. hard labels | Compared the RF with accuracy/precision/recall/F1 only; no RF ROC/PR curve | Open |
101: 
102: **Evidence:** the preparation run prints `0.50% rows deleted`; the 1:1 check is in `../part_1/src/task1`; duplicate and `?` counts recomputed on `datasets/census_income.csv`.
103: 
104: ## 6. Limitations and trade-offs
105: 
106: | Area | Limitation or trade-off | Impact | Mitigation or next step |
107: | --- | --- | --- | --- |
108: | Data | The data is a 1994 US census sample, not a current population | Income levels and feature effects do not transfer to today or to other countries | Treat the model as a historical baseline and document the cohort |
109: | Data | Removing all 244 `capital-gain = 99999` rows may remove a non-random group | If those rows differ systematically, the estimated income rate is biased | Compare results with a missing-indicator encoding instead of deletion |
110: | Data | 29 duplicates and 1–6% `?` values remain | Duplicates can inflate the apparent fit; `?` may be informative missingness | Deduplicate and test an explicit missing-value strategy |
111: | Model | The NN is a regressor, so its scores are not calibrated probabilities (observed range −0.59 to 1.57) | A threshold of 0.362 is not a 36.2% probability of earning more than $50K | Calibrate with isotonic/Platt scaling, or compare `MLPClassifier.predict_proba` |
112: | Model | Both thresholds were chosen on the same test set used to report the metrics | The reported F1 and recall are optimistic; the selection has no independent confirmation | Nested CV: choose thresholds in an inner fold and report on an outer fold |
113: | Evaluation | One 80/20 split (9,720 rows, 2,314 positives) with no confidence intervals | Differences such as RF F1 0.664 vs NN F1 0.689 may be within noise | 5-fold or repeated cross-validation with bootstrap intervals |
114: | Fairness | Sex, race, native-country and marital status are used as predictors; no subgroup metrics were computed | The model may reproduce historical income disparities | Report recall and precision by sex and race before deployment |
115: | Presentation | The five figures cover model evaluation; the education, marital-status and sex income rates are reported as table values, not as labelled EDA charts | The Task 1 expectation that each finding is backed by a chart is only partly met | Add bar charts for income rate by education, marital status and sex, and a feature-importance chart |
116: | Operations | No fitted model is persisted; `run.py` retrains and overwrites outputs | Task 2 cannot serve a stable model version without rerunning training | Save the fitted pipelines and metadata with `joblib` |
117: 
118: **Evidence:** `../part_1/src/task1` (regressor, hard RF labels), `../part_1/src/task1` (sort bug, full-data fit), `../part_1/src/task1` (single split, thresholds on test data).
119:

121: 
122: | Priority | Next step | Why | Effort |
123: | --- | --- | --- | --- |
124: | 1 | Persist the fitted scaler, NN, RF and feature list with `joblib` | Task 2 needs a reproducible artifact rather than retraining on every start | S |
125: | 2 | Replace the single split with 5-fold cross-validation and bootstrap confidence intervals | Confirms whether the RF/NN difference and the threshold choice are stable | M |
126: | 3 | Calibrate the NN scores and evaluate `MLPClassifier` as an alternative | Makes the threshold interpretable as a probability and gives a fair probabilistic baseline | M |
127: | 4 | Deduplicate, test a missing-value strategy and add class weights | Removes the remaining data-quality issues and may improve minority-class recall | S |
128: | 5 | Add subgroup precision/recall by sex and race, plus a small test for the cleaning rules | Makes fairness risks visible and protects the pipeline from regressions | M |

4: def check_one_to_one_correspondence(
5:     df: pd.DataFrame,
6:     col_a: str,
7:     col_b: str,
8: ) -> pd.DataFrame:
9:     """Check whether two columns have a one-to-one correspondence.
10: 
11:     A one-to-one correspondence means each distinct value in ``col_a``
12:     maps to exactly one distinct value in ``col_b`` (and vice versa).
13:     This function returns the subset of rows that violate that rule.
14: 
15:     Parameters
16:     ----------
17:     df : pandas.DataFrame
18:         The input dataframe.
19:     col_a : str
20:         Name of the first column.
21:     col_b : str
22:         Name of the second column.
23: 
24:     Returns
25:     -------
26:     pandas.DataFrame
27:         Rows from ``df`` where the value in ``col_a`` is associated with
28:         more than one value in ``col_b`` or where the value in ``col_b``
29:         is associated with more than one value in ``col_a``.
30:         Returns an empty dataframe if the correspondence is one-to-one.
31:     """
32: 
33:     if col_a not in df.columns or col_b not in df.columns:
34:         raise KeyError(
35:             f"Columns '{col_a}' and '{col_b}' must exist in the dataframe."
36:         )
37: 
38:     # Group by col_a -> set of col_b values
39:     a_to_b = df.groupby(col_a)[col_b].nunique()
40:     bad_a = a_to_b[a_to_b > 1].index
41: 
42:     # Group by col_b -> set of col_a values
43:     b_to_a = df.groupby(col_b)[col_a].nunique()
44:     bad_b = b_to_a[b_to_a > 1].index
45: 
46:     # Rows that break the correspondence in either direction
47:     mask = df[col_a].isin(bad_a) | df[col_b].isin(bad_b)
48:     return df[mask].copy()

43: ## Setup on Windows
44: 
45: On Windows, Docker Desktop runs on WSL 2, and every other tool installs with `winget` from PowerShell. Plan about 45 minutes, including up to one reboot.
46: 
47: 1. **Check for WSL 2 and enable it if needed.** Open PowerShell as Administrator and run:
48: 
49:    ```powershell
50:    wsl --version
51:    ```
52: 
53:    **If it prints version details** (for example `WSL version: 2.x.x`), WSL is already installed. Run `wsl --update` to make sure it's current, then go straight to step 2. No reboot is needed.
54: 
55:    **If you get an error or a list of usage options instead**, WSL is missing or outdated. Install it, then reboot:
56: 
57:    ```powershell
58:    wsl --install
59:    wsl --update
60:    ```
61: 
62:    If the install reports that virtualisation is disabled, enable Intel VT-x or AMD-V in your BIOS/UEFI and run the commands again. You can check this beforehand in Task Manager → Performance → CPU, where "Virtualization" should say *Enabled*.
63: 
64: 2. **Install the tools.** Close VS Code, Git Bash and any other app that uses Git, then open a normal PowerShell window and run:
65: 
66:    ```powershell
67:    winget install -e --id Git.Git
68:    winget install -e --id Docker.DockerDesktop
69:    winget install -e --id Kubernetes.kubectl
70:    winget install -e --id Helm.Helm
71:    winget install -e --id astral-sh.uv
72:    winget install -e --id ezwinports.make   # GNU make, for the starter repo Makefile
73:    ```
74: 
75:    Accept the administrator prompts when they appear. If a tool is already installed, winget upgrades it instead.
76: 
77:    Then open PowerShell **as Administrator** and install minikube, which needs admin rights:
78: 
79:    ```powershell
80:    winget install -e --id Kubernetes.minikube
81:    ```
82: 
83:    If Git fails with `exit code: 4`, a program is still using Git. Close it and run the Git command again.
84: 
85: 3. **Restart PowerShell.** Close every PowerShell window and open a new one so the new `PATH` entries take effect. Otherwise commands like `kubectl` or `uv` will say "not recognized".
86: 
87:    If a command is still "not recognized" later, reinstall that tool and restart PowerShell again. If it's Git and an upgrade failed earlier, the old version was removed before the error: close any app that uses Git, then reinstall from an Administrator PowerShell with `winget install -e --id Git.Git --force`.
88: 
89:    If a command prints an older version than winget installed, another copy comes first in your `PATH`. Run `where.exe <tool>` (for example `where.exe kubectl`) to see every copy. Docker Desktop includes its own `kubectl`, so an older `kubectl` version is expected and fine.
90: 
91: 4. **Start Docker Desktop** from the Start menu (not with "Run as administrator"), accept the terms, and check that *Settings → General → Choose Virtual Machine Manager (VMM)* is set to **WSL 2**. Older versions show this as a *Use the WSL 2 based engine* checkbox, which should be ticked.
92: 
93:    If Docker Desktop says the *Privileged helper service is not running*, click *Start* and accept the administrator prompt. If it asks every time, run `Set-Service com.docker.service -StartupType Automatic` in an Administrator PowerShell.
94: 
95:    If Docker Desktop closes with `open \\.\pipe\docker_engine: Access is denied`, another program is using Docker's connection. Restart Windows and start Docker Desktop again. If you also have Podman Desktop or Rancher Desktop, quit them first, since they conflict with Docker Desktop.
96: 
97: 5. **Give WSL enough memory.** With the WSL 2 engine, Docker's memory is set by WSL, not by Docker Desktop. Open the config file in Notepad:
98: 
99:    ```powershell
100:    notepad "$env:USERPROFILE\.wslconfig"
101:    ```
102: 
103:    If Notepad asks to create the file, choose *Yes*. Add the content below and save. Set `memory` to about half your computer's RAM, for example `8GB` on a 16 GB laptop:
104: 
105:    ```ini
106:    [wsl2]
107:    memory=8GB
108:    processors=4
109:    ```
110: 
111:    Then run `wsl --shutdown` and restart Docker Desktop. This stops Docker and any running containers, so do it before you start working.
112: 
113: 6. **Install Python 3.12 through uv:**
114: 
115:    ```powershell
116:    uv python install 3.12
117:    ```
118: 
119: 7. **Configure Git** (use the email of your GitHub account):
120: 
121:    ```powershell
122:    git config --global user.name "Your Name"
123:    git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
124:    ```
125: 
126: Then continue with *Verify your setup*.
127: 
128: **Shell scripts:** Git for Windows includes *Git Bash*. Use it for any `.sh` script in the starter repository.
129: 
130: **Prefer Linux tools?** You can work inside an Ubuntu distribution in WSL. If you had WSL before this setup, you may not have Ubuntu yet: check with `wsl --list`, and install it with `wsl --install -d Ubuntu` if it's missing. Keep Docker Desktop on Windows, enable *Settings → Resources → WSL integration* for Ubuntu, then follow the Ubuntu section inside WSL, skipping the Docker Engine step. Keep your repository inside the WSL file system (`~/`), not under `/mnt/c`, or file access becomes slow.

222: ## Verify your setup
223: 
224: Your setup is ready when every command below succeeds and the minikube node reports `Ready`. The commands are the same on all three systems (PowerShell, macOS Terminal or Linux shell).
225: 
226: 1. **Check versions.** Every command should print a version, not an error.
227: 
228:    ```bash
229:    git --version
230:    docker version
231:    docker compose version
232:    minikube version
233:    kubectl version --client
234:    helm version
235:    uv --version
236:    make --version
237:    ```
238: 2. **Check Docker can run containers:**
239: 
240:    ```bash
241:    docker run --rm hello-world
242:    ```
243: 3. **Start the cluster** (the first start downloads about 1 GB, so do it at home):
244: 
245:    ```bash
246:    minikube start --driver=docker --cpus=4 --memory=6144
247:    kubectl get nodes          # STATUS should be Ready
248:    kubectl get pods -A        # system pods Running
249:    helm list -A               # empty list, no error
250:    ```
251: 4. **Deploy and reach a test service**, then remove it. On Windows and macOS, `minikube service` keeps the terminal busy while the tunnel is open; press Ctrl+C when done.
252: 
253:    ```bash
254:    kubectl create deployment hello --image=nginx:alpine
255:    kubectl expose deployment hello --port=80 --type=NodePort
256:    minikube service hello --url
257:    kubectl delete service,deployment hello
258:    ```
259: 5. **Check Python and uv** in a throwaway project:
260: 
261:    ```bash
262:    uv init env-check --python 3.12
263:    cd env-check
264:    uv add pandas
265:    uv run python -c "import sys, pandas; print(sys.version, pandas.__version__)"
266:    ```
267: 6. **Run the starter repository check** once you have cloned it: `make check`.
268: 7. **Pre-pull images and data.** Pull the base images you plan to use (for example `docker pull python:3.12-slim`) and any images listed in the starter repository README, and download your dataset.
269: 
270: ### Getting your own images into minikube
271: 
272: minikube runs its own container runtime, so an image you build with plain `docker build` is not visible to the cluster. Use one of these:
273: 
274: - `minikube image build -t myapp:dev .` builds straight into the cluster.
275: - `minikube image load myapp:dev` copies an image you already built.
276: 
277: In your manifests, set `imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent` (or `Never`) for local images, and use a tag other than `latest`.
278: 
279: ### Stopping and resetting
280: 
281: - `minikube stop` pauses the cluster and keeps its state; `minikube start` resumes it.
282: - `minikube delete` wipes the cluster completely. Use it only when you want a clean slate.

| Topic | Decision | Reason |

| Cleaned dataset | Generate `part_1/dataset/census_clean.csv` from the raw CSV | Keeps raw data untouched and gives Task 2 its own reproducible input |

| RF comparison | Add RF probabilities to Task 1 artefacts (recommended); fall back to hard labels if skipped | A shared threshold is much more useful for comparing the two models |

from __future__ import annotations

import pandas as pd

SENTINEL_VALUE = 99999
SENTINEL_COLUMNS = ("capital-gain", "capital-loss")

DROP_COLUMNS = ("fnlwgt", "education-num")

CATEGORICAL_FEATURES = (
    "workclass",
    "education",
    "marital-status",
    "occupation",
    "relationship",
    "race",
    "sex",
    "native-country",
)

MISSING_COLUMNS = ("workclass", "occupation", "native-country")
MISSING_MARKER = "?"
UNKNOWN_VALUE = "Unknown"

TARGET_SOURCE_COLUMN = "income"
TARGET_COLUMN = "target"
TARGET_COLUMNS = (TARGET_SOURCE_COLUMN, TARGET_COLUMN)
ALLOWED_INCOME_VALUES = ("<=50K", ">50K")

RAW_COLUMN_ORDER = (
    "age",
    "workclass",
    "fnlwgt",
    "education",
    "education-num",
    "marital-status",
    "occupation",
    "relationship",
    "race",
    "sex",
    "capital-gain",
    "capital-loss",
    "hours-per-week",
    "native-country",
    "income",
)

CLEAN_COLUMN_ORDER = (
    "age",
    "workclass",
    "education",
    "marital-status",
    "occupation",
    "relationship",
    "race",
    "sex",
    "capital-gain",
    "capital-loss",
    "hours-per-week",
    "native-country",
    "income",
    "target",
)


def _normalise_columns(df: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Return a copy with stripped column names and no duplicate names."""
    normalised = df.copy()
    normalised.columns = [str(column).strip() for column in normalised.columns]

    duplicated = normalised.columns[normalised.columns.duplicated()].tolist()
    if duplicated:
        raise ValueError(
            "Duplicate column names after stripping whitespace: "
            f"{sorted(set(duplicated))}"
        )

    return normalised


def _require_raw_columns(df: pd.DataFrame) -> None:
    missing = [column for column in RAW_COLUMN_ORDER if column not in df.columns]
    if missing:
        raise KeyError(f"Missing required raw columns: {missing}")


def _strip_categorical_values(df: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Strip whitespace from categorical values; the caller owns the copy."""
    for column in CATEGORICAL_FEATURES:
        df[column] = df[column].astype("string").str.strip()
    return df


def _sentinel_mask(df: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.Series:
    mask = pd.Series(False, index=df.index, dtype=bool)
    for column in SENTINEL_COLUMNS:
        mask |= df[column].eq(SENTINEL_VALUE)
    return mask


def numeric_columns(df: pd.DataFrame) -> list[str]:
    """Return numeric feature columns, excluding the target representations."""
    return [
        column
        for column in df.columns
        if column not in TARGET_COLUMNS
        and pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(df[column])
    ]


def categorical_columns(df: pd.DataFrame) -> list[str]:
    """Return categorical feature columns, excluding the target representations."""
    return [
        column
        for column in df.columns
        if column not in TARGET_COLUMNS
        and not pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(df[column])
    ]


def clean_census(df: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Clean the raw Adult Census Income data without one-hot encoding.

    The returned frame keeps categorical features as strings. Sentinel value
    rows are removed, ``fnlwgt`` and ``education-num`` are dropped, ``?`` is
    replaced with ``Unknown``, and ``income`` is normalised into a string plus
    a boolean ``target`` column.

    Parameters
    ----------
    df:
        Raw or already column-stripped census data. The input is not mutated.

    Returns
    -------
    pandas.DataFrame
        Cleaned data with ``CLEAN_COLUMN_ORDER`` columns.
    """
    prepared = _normalise_columns(df)
    _require_raw_columns(prepared)
    prepared = _strip_categorical_values(prepared)

    cleaned = prepared.loc[~_sentinel_mask(prepared)].copy()
    cleaned = cleaned.drop(columns=list(DROP_COLUMNS))

    for column in MISSING_COLUMNS:
        cleaned[column] = cleaned[column].mask(
            cleaned[column].eq(MISSING_MARKER),
            UNKNOWN_VALUE,
        )

    income = (
        cleaned[TARGET_SOURCE_COLUMN]
        .astype("string")
        .str.strip()
        .str.rstrip(".")
    )

    if income.isna().any():
        raise ValueError("The income column contains missing values.")

    unexpected = sorted(set(income.unique()) - set(ALLOWED_INCOME_VALUES))
    if unexpected:
        raise ValueError(
            "Unexpected income values after normalisation: "
            f"{unexpected}. Expected only {list(ALLOWED_INCOME_VALUES)}."
        )

    cleaned[TARGET_SOURCE_COLUMN] = income
    cleaned[TARGET_COLUMN] = income.eq(">50K").fillna(False).astype(bool)

    return cleaned.loc[:, list(CLEAN_COLUMN_ORDER)].reset_index(drop=True).copy()


def cleaning_summary(raw_df: pd.DataFrame, clean_df: pd.DataFrame) -> dict:
    """Describe the effect of :func:`clean_census` on the raw data."""
    raw = _normalise_columns(raw_df)
    _require_raw_columns(raw)
    raw = _strip_categorical_values(raw)

    rows_before = len(raw)
    rows_after = len(clean_df)
    sentinel_mask = _sentinel_mask(raw)

    sentinel_counts = {
        column: int(raw[column].eq(SENTINEL_VALUE).sum())
        for column in SENTINEL_COLUMNS
    }
    missing_markers_raw = {
        column: int(raw[column].eq(MISSING_MARKER).sum())
        for column in MISSING_COLUMNS
    }
    missing_markers_cleaned = {
        column: int(clean_df[column].astype("string").eq(UNKNOWN_VALUE).sum())
        for column in MISSING_COLUMNS
    }

    positive_count = int(clean_df[TARGET_COLUMN].sum())
    negative_count = rows_after - positive_count

    return {
        "rows_before": rows_before,
        "rows_after": rows_after,
        "rows_removed": rows_before - rows_after,
        "rows_removed_sentinel": int(sentinel_mask.sum()),
        "sentinel_counts": sentinel_counts,
        "positive_count": positive_count,
        "negative_count": negative_count,
        "positive_rate": positive_count / rows_after if rows_after else 0.0,
        "columns": list(clean_df.columns),
        "numeric_columns": numeric_columns(clean_df),
        "categorical_columns": categorical_columns(clean_df),
        "target_columns": list(TARGET_COLUMNS),
        "missing_markers_raw": missing_markers_raw,
        "missing_markers_cleaned": missing_markers_cleaned,
    }


__all__ = [
    "ALLOWED_INCOME_VALUES",
    "CATEGORICAL_FEATURES",
    "CLEAN_COLUMN_ORDER",
    "DROP_COLUMNS",
    "MISSING_COLUMNS",
    "MISSING_MARKER",
    "RAW_COLUMN_ORDER",
    "SENTINEL_COLUMNS",
    "SENTINEL_VALUE",
    "TARGET_COLUMN",
    "TARGET_COLUMNS",
    "TARGET_SOURCE_COLUMN",
    "UNKNOWN_VALUE",
    "categorical_columns",
    "clean_census",
    "cleaning_summary",
    "numeric_columns",
]

from __future__ import annotations

import json
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd

from task2.cleaning import clean_census, cleaning_summary

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
REPO_ROOT = ROOT.parent

RAW_PATH = REPO_ROOT / "datasets" / "census_income.csv"
OUTPUT_DIR = ROOT / "dataset"
OUTPUT_PATH = OUTPUT_DIR / "census_clean.csv"
METADATA_PATH = OUTPUT_DIR / "census_clean_meta.json"


def main() -> int:
    raw = pd.read_csv(RAW_PATH, encoding="utf-8")
    cleaned = clean_census(raw)

    summary = cleaning_summary(raw, cleaned)
    summary = {
        "source": RAW_PATH.relative_to(REPO_ROOT).as_posix(),
        **summary,
    }

    OUTPUT_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    cleaned.to_csv(OUTPUT_PATH, index=False)
    METADATA_PATH.write_text(
        json.dumps(summary, indent=2) + "\n",
        encoding="utf-8",
    )

    print(f"Raw rows: {summary['rows_before']:,}")
    print(
        "Rows removed (sentinel values): "
        f"{summary['rows_removed_sentinel']:,}"
    )
    print(f"Cleaned rows: {summary['rows_after']:,}")
    print(
        "Positive class: "
        f"{summary['positive_count']:,} "
        f"({summary['positive_rate'] * 100:.2f}%)"
    )
    print(f"Saved: {OUTPUT_PATH}")
    print(f"Saved metadata: {METADATA_PATH}")

    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())

            "relationship_",
            "race_",
            "sex_",

## Requirements
- Clean dataset: remove sentinel values (`capital-gain == 99999`), drop `fnlwgt` and `education-num`.

- Dashboard must show: the cleaned table, feature histograms, feature correlations; user selects visualization type and features.
- Model page: threshold slider changes confusion matrix; toggle compares with random forest.

from __future__ import annotations

import os

import dash_bootstrap_components as dbc
import pandas as pd
from dash import Dash, html

from .data import PredictionData, load_clean_dataset, load_predictions

DEFAULT_HOST = "0.0.0.0"
DEFAULT_PORT = 8050
DEFAULT_DEBUG = False

DATA_SOURCE_NOTE = (
    "Data source: Adult Census Income (datasets/census_income.csv), cleaned to "
    "part_1/dataset/census_clean.csv. Model metrics use the Task 1 held-out "
    "test set."
)


def _env_flag(name: str, default: bool = False) -> bool:
    raw = os.environ.get(name)
    if raw is None:
        return default
    return raw.strip().lower() in {"1", "true", "yes", "on"}


def _build_layout(dataset: pd.DataFrame, predictions: PredictionData) -> dbc.Container:
    positive_rate = float(dataset["target"].mean())

    header = dbc.Container(
        [
            html.H1(
                "Adult Census Income Explorer",
                className="display-6 mb-1",
            ),
            html.P(
                "Explore the cleaned census data and the Task 1 models on "
                "held-out data.",
                className="lead text-muted mb-0",
            ),
        ],
        fluid=True,
        className="py-3",
    )

    data_tab = dbc.Card(
        [
            dbc.CardHeader("Data explorer"),
            dbc.CardBody(
                [
                    html.H5("Interactive exploration", className="card-title"),
                    html.P(
                        "The table view, feature histograms, and correlation "
                        "views will be added in the next prompts.",
                        className="card-text",
                    ),
                    html.P(
                        [
                            html.Strong(f"{len(dataset):,}"),
                            " rows · ",
                            html.Strong(f"{len(dataset.columns)}"),
                            " columns · ",
                            html.Strong(f"{positive_rate:.2%}"),
                            " positive class",
                        ],
                        className="text-muted mb-0",
                    ),
                ]
            ),
        ],
        className="shadow-sm",
    )

    model_tab = dbc.Card(
        [
            dbc.CardHeader("Model evaluation"),
            dbc.CardBody(
                [
                    html.H5("Thresholded model comparison", className="card-title"),
                    html.P(
                        "The score threshold, confusion matrices, and random "
                        "forest comparison will be added in the next prompts.",
                        className="card-text",
                    ),
                    html.P(
                        [
                            "Evaluation set: ",
                            html.Strong(f"{predictions.size:,}"),
                            " held-out rows",
                        ],
                        className="text-muted mb-0",
                    ),
                ]
            ),
        ],
        className="shadow-sm",
    )

    tabs = dbc.Tabs(
        [
            dbc.Tab(data_tab, label="Data explorer", tab_id="data-explorer"),
            dbc.Tab(model_tab, label="Model evaluation", tab_id="model-evaluation"),
        ],
        id="main-tabs",
        active_tab="data-explorer",
        className="mb-3",
    )

    footer = html.Footer(
        html.P(DATA_SOURCE_NOTE, className="text-muted small mb-0"),
        className="mt-4 pt-3 border-top",
    )

    return dbc.Container(
        [header, tabs, footer],
        fluid=True,
        className="px-3 px-md-4 pb-4",
    )


def create_app(
    data_path: str | None = None,
    pred_dir: str | None = None,
) -> Dash:
    """Create the Dash application and load its data exactly once."""
    dataset = load_clean_dataset(data_path)
    predictions = load_predictions(pred_dir)

    app = Dash(
        __name__,
        external_stylesheets=[dbc.themes.BOOTSTRAP],
        title="Adult Census Income Explorer",
    )
    app.layout = _build_layout(dataset, predictions)

    @app.server.route("/health")
    def health() -> dict[str, str]:
        return {"status": "ok"}

    return app


app = create_app()
server = app.server


def main() -> None:
    """Run the development server using environment-based configuration."""
    host = os.environ.get("HOST", DEFAULT_HOST)
    port = int(os.environ.get("PORT", DEFAULT_PORT))
    debug = _env_flag("DASH_DEBUG", DEFAULT_DEBUG)

    app.run(host=host, port=port, debug=debug)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

from __future__ import annotations

import json
import os
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
REPO_ROOT = ROOT.parent

RAW_PATH = REPO_ROOT / "datasets" / "census_income.csv"


def _ensure_clean_dataset() -> Path:
    """Create the cleaned dataset when it is missing and return its path."""
    from task2.data import DATA_PATH_ENV, DEFAULT_DATA_PATH

    data_path = Path(os.environ.get(DATA_PATH_ENV, DEFAULT_DATA_PATH))
    if data_path.exists():
        return data_path

    from task2.cleaning import clean_census, cleaning_summary

    raw = pd.read_csv(RAW_PATH, encoding="utf-8")
    cleaned = clean_census(raw)

    summary = {
        "source": RAW_PATH.relative_to(REPO_ROOT).as_posix(),
        **cleaning_summary(raw, cleaned),
    }

    data_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    cleaned.to_csv(data_path, index=False)

    meta_path = data_path.with_name(f"{data_path.stem}_meta.json")
    meta_path.write_text(
        json.dumps(summary, indent=2) + "\n",
        encoding="utf-8",
    )

    print(
        "Cleaned dataset not found; generated it automatically.\n"
        f"  Raw rows: {summary['rows_before']:,}\n"
        f"  Rows removed (sentinel values): "
        f"{summary['rows_removed_sentinel']:,}\n"
        f"  Cleaned rows: {summary['rows_after']:,}\n"
        f"  Positive class: {summary['positive_count']:,} "
        f"({summary['positive_rate'] * 100:.2f}%)\n"
        f"  Saved: {data_path}\n"
        f"  Saved metadata: {meta_path}"
    )

    return data_path


def main() -> int:
    _ensure_clean_dataset()

    import task2

    task2.main()
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())

def _build_histograms(
    dataset: pd.DataFrame,
    selected_features: list[str] | None,
    split_by_target: bool = False,
) -> html.Div | dbc.Alert:
    features = _valid_features(dataset, selected_features)

    if not features:
        return dbc.Alert(
            "Select at least one feature to plot a distribution.",
            color="warning",
            className="mb-0",
        )

    if len(features) > MAX_HISTOGRAM_FEATURES:
        return dbc.Alert(
            "Select at most four features to compare distributions",
            color="warning",
            className="mb-0",
        )

    n_cols = min(2, len(features))
    n_rows = ceil(len(features) / n_cols)
    subplot_titles = [pretty_column_name(feature) for feature in features]

    subplot_kwargs: dict[str, float] = {}
    if n_rows > 1:
        subplot_kwargs["vertical_spacing"] = 0.16
    if n_cols > 1:
        subplot_kwargs["horizontal_spacing"] = 0.12

    figure = make_subplots(
        rows=n_rows,
        cols=n_cols,
        subplot_titles=subplot_titles,
        **subplot_kwargs,
    )

    for index, feature in enumerate(features):
        row = index // n_cols + 1
        column = index % n_cols + 1
        title = pretty_column_name(feature)
        show_legend = split_by_target and index == 0

        if _is_numeric_feature(dataset, feature):
            if split_by_target:
                for target_value in (False, True):
                    figure.add_trace(
                        go.Histogram(
                            x=dataset.loc[
                                dataset["target"].eq(target_value), feature
                            ],
                            nbinsx=HISTOGRAM_BINS,
                            name=TARGET_LABELS[target_value],
                            marker_color=TARGET_COLORS[target_value],
                            opacity=0.6,
                            showlegend=show_legend,
                        ),
                        row=row,
                        col=column,
                    )
            else:
                figure.add_trace(
                    go.Histogram(
                        x=dataset[feature],
                        nbinsx=HISTOGRAM_BINS,
                        name=title,
                        marker_color="#4c78a8",
                        showlegend=False,
                    ),
                    row=row,
                    col=column,
                )
            figure.update_xaxes(title_text=title, row=row, col=column)
        else:
            if split_by_target:
                counts = pd.crosstab(dataset[feature], dataset["target"])
                counts = counts.reindex(
                    columns=[False, True],
                    fill_value=0,
                )
                counts = counts.loc[
                    counts.sum(axis=1).sort_values(ascending=False).index
                ]
                x_values = _category_labels(counts.index, feature)

                for target_value in (False, True):
                    figure.add_trace(
                        go.Bar(
                            x=x_values,
                            y=counts[target_value],
                            name=TARGET_LABELS[target_value],
                            marker_color=TARGET_COLORS[target_value],
                            showlegend=show_legend,
                        ),
                        row=row,
                        col=column,
                    )
            else:
                counts = dataset[feature].value_counts()
                figure.add_trace(
                    go.Bar(
                        x=_category_labels(counts.index, feature),
                        y=counts.to_numpy(),
                        name=title,
                        marker_color="#4c78a8",
                        showlegend=False,
                    ),
                    row=row,
                    col=column,
                )
            figure.update_xaxes(
                title_text=title,
                tickangle=-45,
                row=row,
                col=column,
            )

        figure.update_yaxes(
            title_text="Count",
            row=row,
            col=column,
        )

    if len(features) < n_rows * n_cols:
        figure.update_xaxes(visible=False, row=n_rows, col=n_cols)
        figure.update_yaxes(visible=False, row=n_rows, col=n_cols)

    figure.update_layout(
        title_text=(
            "Feature distributions split by income"
            if split_by_target
            else "Feature distributions"
        ),
        height=320 * n_rows,
        margin={"l": 60, "r": 20, "t": 70, "b": 60},
        bargap=0.05,
        barmode="group",
        showlegend=split_by_target,
    )
    if split_by_target:
        figure.update_layout(legend_title_text="Income")

    note = (
        "Numeric features use 30-bin histograms; categorical features use "
        "value-count bars sorted from most to least frequent."
    )
    if split_by_target:
        note = (
            "Distributions are split by observed income class; numeric "
            "histograms are overlaid at 60% opacity and categorical bars are "
            "grouped."
        )

    return html.Div(
        [
            dcc.Graph(
                figure=figure,
                config={"displaylogo": False, "responsive": True},
            ),
            html.P(note, className="text-muted small mt-2 mb-0"),
        ]
    )
```

from task2.app import _build_correlation
from task2.data import load_clean_dataset
from task2.metrics import cramers_v, cramers_v_matrix, pearson_correlation

dataset = load_clean_dataset()

# Metric helpers
numeric = ['age', 'capital-gain', 'capital-loss', 'hours-per-week']
corr = pearson_correlation(dataset, numeric)
print('pearson shape:', corr.shape)
print('pearson symmetric:', corr.round(10).equals(corr.T.round(10)))
print('pearson diagonal:', [round(float(corr.loc[c, c]), 6) for c in numeric])
print('pearson range:', float(corr.min().min()), float(corr.max().max()))

categorical = ['workclass', 'education', 'marital-status', 'occupation', 'relationship', 'race', 'sex', 'native-country']
v_matrix = cramers_v_matrix(dataset, categorical)
print('\ncramer shape:', v_matrix.shape)
print('cramer symmetric:', v_matrix.round(10).equals(v_matrix.T.round(10)))
print('cramer diagonal:', [round(float(v_matrix.loc[c, c]), 6) for c in categorical])
print('cramer min/max:', float(v_matrix.min().min()), float(v_matrix.max().max()))
print('cramer pair sex/relationship:', round(cramers_v(dataset['sex'], dataset['relationship']), 6))

# Zero-denominator case
constant = dataset['sex'].copy()
constant[:] = 'Male'
print('constant cramer:', cramers_v(constant, dataset['relationship']))

# Rendering
def fig_from(result):
    assert isinstance(result, html.Div), type(result).__name__
    return result.children[0].figure

numeric_result = _build_correlation(dataset, ['age', 'hours-per-week'], 'numeric')
print('\nnumeric result type:', type(numeric_result).__name__)
fig = fig_from(numeric_result)
print('numeric title:', fig.layout.title.text)
print('numeric zmin/zmax:', fig.data[0].zmin, fig.data[0].zmax)
print('numeric colorscale type:', type(fig.data[0].colorscale).__name__)
print('numeric x labels:', list(fig.data[0].x))
print('numeric y labels:', list(fig.data[0].y))
print('numeric texttemplate:', fig.data[0].texttemplate)
print('numeric colorbar title:', fig.data[0].colorbar.title.text)
print('numeric xaxis title:', fig.layout.xaxis.title.text)
print('numeric yaxis title:', fig.layout.yaxis.title.text)

categorical_result = _build_correlation(dataset, ['sex', 'relationship'], 'categorical')
print('\ncategorical result type:', type(categorical_result).__name__)
fig = fig_from(categorical_result)
print('categorical title:', fig.layout.title.text)
print('categorical zmin/zmax:', fig.data[0].zmin, fig.data[0].zmax)
print('categorical x labels:', list(fig.data[0].x))
print('categorical z:', fig.data[0].z.tolist())
print('categorical colorbar title:', fig.data[0].colorbar.title.text)

# Alerts
print('\nno numeric features:', type(_build_correlation(dataset, ['sex', 'relationship'], 'numeric')).__name__)
print('no categorical features:', type(_build_correlation(dataset, ['age', 'hours-per-week'], 'categorical')).__name__)
print('empty selection:', type(_build_correlation(dataset, [], 'numeric')).__name__)

19:     The value is derived from a contingency table, so the categorical values
20:     are never one-hot encoded. The result is clamped to ``[0, 1]`` to absorb
21:     floating-point noise.

32:     )

36:     value = float(np.sqrt(chi2 / denominator))
37:     return min(max(value, 0.0), 1.0)

## Objective
- Build Part 1 Task 2 incrementally from `.opencode/plan/task2_plan.md`: an interactive Dash dashboard for data exploration and Task 1 model evaluation, then containerize/deploy it.
- The user is executing the prompts one at a time and has now requested Prompt 7.

## Requirements
- Do not commit to git.
- Do not update `part_1/AI_LOG.md`.
- Clean dataset: remove sentinel rows (`capital-gain == 99999`), drop `fnlwgt` and `education-num`, keep categorical features as strings without one-hot encoding.
- Dashboard must show the cleaned table, feature histograms, and feature correlations, with user-selected visualization type and features.
- Model page: threshold slider changes the NN confusion matrix; toggle compares with random forest.
- `run_dashboard.py` must create the cleaned dataset if it does not exist before starting the app.
- Prompt 2 was skipped, so RF comparison must use saved hard labels at 0.5 and clearly label that limitation.
- The dashboard reads saved CSV artifacts and never retrains models.

## Decisions
- Cleaned output: `part_1/dataset/census_clean.csv` plus `part_1/dataset/census_clean_meta.json`.
- Keep normalized `income` strings and add boolean `target`.
- Two tabs: **Data explorer** and **Model evaluation**.
- Use saved prediction artifacts as the reproducible source; do not hardcode Task 1 report metrics.
- Optional histogram split-by-target switch was implemented and defaults off.
- `scipy` was added as an explicit dependency via `uv add scipy`.

## Work State
### Completed
- Prompt 0 baseline audit completed.
- Prompt 1 completed: cleaning module, CLI, tests, generated dataset/metadata, `.gitignore` entries.
- Prompt 2 explicitly skipped.
- Prompt 3 completed: data layer, Dash app shell, `/health`, `run_dashboard.py` auto-generation.
- Prompt 4 completed: interactive table with column selection, sorting, filtering, pagination, CSV export, target labels.
- Prompt 5 completed: numeric histograms, categorical bar charts, 1–4 feature grid, alerts, optional split-by-target.
- Prompt 6 completed: Pearson and Cramér's V correlation heatmaps, method radio control, `metrics.py` correlation helpers.
- Existing 11 tests pass.

### Active
- Prompt 7 requested but not yet implemented: model evaluation tab with threshold slider, NN confusion matrix, metric cards, RF comparison, and tests.

### Blocked
- None technically blocking; the Task 1 report/threshold discrepancy must be documented during Prompt 7.

## Next Move
1. Add `confusion_metrics(y_true, y_score, threshold)` to `part_1/src/task2/metrics.py`, using `y_score > threshold`.
2. Build the Model evaluation tab in `part_1/src/task2/app.py` with `threshold-slider`, `compare-rf`, NN/RF confusion matrices, metric cards, counts, comparison table, notes, and `dcc.Loading`.
3. Add callbacks for threshold changes and RF comparison, using hard-label RF fallback at 0.5 when `rf_has_proba` is false.
4. Add tests for a hand-computed confusion matrix and real NN metrics at threshold `0.362`.
5. Smoke-test `/health`, callbacks, and the running dashboard; run the test suite.
6. Do not commit and do not update `AI_LOG.md`.

## Relevant Files
- `part_1/src/task2/app.py`: Dash layout and callbacks; Prompt 7 changes belong here.
- `part_1/src/task2/metrics.py`: correlation helpers exist; add confusion metrics here.
- `part_1/src/task2/data.py`: loads cleaned data and prediction artifacts.
- `part_1/tests/test_task2.py`: existing tests; extend for metrics.
- `part_1/data/nn_pred.csv`: NN continuous scores and `real` labels.
- `part_1/data/rf_pred.csv`: RF hard labels only, no `proba`.
- `part_1/data/nn_roc.csv`: saved ROC curve.
- `part_1/data/nn_prc.csv`: saved PR curve.
- `part_1/run_dashboard.py`: ensures cleaned dataset exists, then runs app.
- `part_1/src/task2/cleaning.py`: cleaning rules and helpers.
- `part_1/pyproject.toml`: Dash/DBC/Plotly/SciPy dependencies.
- `reports/task1.md`: Task 1 report; threshold/metrics conflict with saved artifacts.
- `.opencode/plan/task2_plan.md`: Prompt 7 requirements and acceptance checks.

## Important Context
- Cleaned dataset: **48,598 rows × 14 columns**, **11,443 positives (23.55%)**.
- Cleaned columns: `age, workclass, education, marital-status, occupation, relationship, race, sex, capital-gain, capital-loss, hours-per-week, native-country, income, target`.
- Test set: **9,720 rows**, 7,406 negatives / 2,314 positives.
- NN scores range **−0.771506 to 1.709464**; slider range must cover this combined range.
- RF artifact has no probabilities; use hard labels fixed at the 0.5 cut-off and label it.
- At `0.362` with `nn_score > threshold`: TP 1,742 / FP 997 / FN 572 / TN 6,409; accuracy 83.86%, precision 63.60%, recall 75.28%, F1 0.6895.
- Task 1 report claims 0.362 but its metrics (≈84.10%, 64.49%, 73.94%, F1 0.6889) match threshold ≈0.3776 in the saved predictions.
- Saved PR best threshold is `0.388066`; saved ROC best threshold is `0.275198`.
- Existing explorer IDs: `viz-type`, `feature-select`, `select-all`, `clear-features`, `split-by-target`, `corr-method`, `explorer-output`.
- All changes are uncommitted; generated `part_1/dataset/census_clean.csv` and metadata are ignored by git.

105: def load_predictions(pred_dir: str | Path | None = None) -> PredictionData:
106:     """Load the Task 1 predictions and align the two model outputs.
107: 
108:     The NN file contains continuous regressor scores. The RF file contains
109:     hard labels in the current artefacts; if a ``proba`` column is added
110:     later, it is used automatically.
111:     """
112:     predictions_dir = _resolve_predictions_dir(pred_dir)
113: 
114:     nn = _read_prediction_file(predictions_dir / NN_PREDICTIONS_FILE)
115:     rf = _read_prediction_file(predictions_dir / RF_PREDICTIONS_FILE)
116: 
117:     required_columns = {"real", "pred"}
118:     for name, frame in (("nn_pred.csv", nn), ("rf_pred.csv", rf)):
119:         missing = required_columns - set(frame.columns)
120:         if missing:
121:             raise ValueError(
122:                 f"{name} is missing required columns: {sorted(missing)}"
123:             )
124: 
125:     if not nn.index.equals(rf.index):
126:         raise ValueError(
127:             "nn_pred.csv and rf_pred.csv are not in the same row order."
128:         )
129: 
130:     y_true = nn["real"].astype(int).to_numpy()
131:     rf_y_true = rf["real"].astype(int).to_numpy()
132: 
133:     if not np.array_equal(y_true, rf_y_true):
134:         raise ValueError(
135:             "nn_pred.csv and rf_pred.csv do not contain the same real labels."
136:         )
137: 
138:     nn_score = nn["pred"].astype(float).to_numpy()
139: 
140:     rf_has_proba = "proba" in rf.columns
141:     if rf_has_proba:
142:         rf_score = rf["proba"].astype(float).to_numpy()
143:     else:
144:         rf_score = rf["pred"].astype(int).to_numpy()
145: 
146:     combined = np.concatenate([nn_score, rf_score])
147:     if combined.min() < DEFAULT_THRESHOLD < combined.max():
148:         threshold_default = DEFAULT_THRESHOLD
149:     else:
150:         threshold_default = FALLBACK_THRESHOLD
151: 
152:     return PredictionData(
153:         y_true=y_true,
154:         nn_score=nn_score,
155:         rf_score=rf_score,
156:         rf_has_proba=rf_has_proba,
157:         threshold_default=threshold_default,
158:     )

def pearson_correlation(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    columns: list[str],
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Return the Pearson correlation matrix for the given columns."""
    return df.loc[:, list(columns)].corr(method="pearson")


def confusion_metrics(
    y_true: np.ndarray,
    y_score: np.ndarray,
    threshold: float,
) -> dict[str, int | float]:
    """Return thresholded confusion-matrix counts and summary metrics.

    A row is predicted positive when ``y_score > threshold``. The strict
    comparison matches the Task 1 evaluation code, so a score exactly equal
    to the threshold is classified as negative. This keeps the dashboard
    consistent with the saved Task 1 artefacts.

    Zero denominators (for example, no predicted positives) produce ``0.0``
    instead of raising an error.
    """
    truth = np.asarray(y_true).astype(bool)
    scores = np.asarray(y_score, dtype=float)

    if truth.shape != scores.shape:
        raise ValueError("y_true and y_score must have the same shape.")

    predicted = scores > threshold

    tp = int(np.sum(predicted & truth))
    fp = int(np.sum(predicted & ~truth))
    fn = int(np.sum(~predicted & truth))
    tn = int(np.sum(~predicted & ~truth))

    total = tp + fp + fn + tn
    accuracy = (tp + tn) / total if total else 0.0
    precision = tp / (tp + fp) if tp + fp else 0.0
    recall = tp / (tp + fn) if tp + fn else 0.0
    f1 = (
        2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall)
        if precision + recall
        else 0.0
    )

    return {
        "tn": tn,
        "fp": fp,
        "fn": fn,
        "tp": tp,
        "accuracy": float(accuracy),
        "precision": float(precision),
        "recall": float(recall),
        "f1": float(f1),
        "predicted_positive": tp + fp,
    }

class ConfusionMetricsTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_hand_computed_confusion_matrix(self) -> None:
        y_true = [0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 0]
        y_score = [0.10, 0.60, 0.60, 0.40, 0.90, 0.50]

        metrics = confusion_metrics(y_true, y_score, threshold=0.5)

        self.assertEqual(metrics["tp"], 2)
        self.assertEqual(metrics["fp"], 1)
        self.assertEqual(metrics["fn"], 1)
        self.assertEqual(metrics["tn"], 2)
        self.assertEqual(metrics["predicted_positive"], 3)
        self.assertAlmostEqual(float(metrics["accuracy"]), 4 / 6)
        self.assertAlmostEqual(float(metrics["precision"]), 2 / 3)
        self.assertAlmostEqual(float(metrics["recall"]), 2 / 3)
        self.assertAlmostEqual(float(metrics["f1"]), 2 / 3)

    def test_threshold_comparison_is_strict(self) -> None:
        metrics = confusion_metrics(
            [0, 1],
            [0.5, 0.5],
            threshold=0.5,
        )

        self.assertEqual(metrics["predicted_positive"], 0)
        self.assertEqual(metrics["fn"], 1)
        self.assertEqual(metrics["tn"], 1)
        self.assertEqual(float(metrics["precision"]), 0.0)
        self.assertEqual(float(metrics["recall"]), 0.0)
        self.assertEqual(float(metrics["f1"]), 0.0)

    def test_real_nn_metrics_at_default_threshold(self) -> None:
        predictions = load_predictions()

        metrics = confusion_metrics(
            predictions.y_true,
            predictions.nn_score,
            threshold=0.362,

        self.assertEqual(metrics["fp"], 997)
        self.assertEqual(metrics["fn"], 572)

            float(metrics["precision"]),

        self.assertAlmostEqual(

            delta=0.001,

        self.assertAlmostEqual(
            float(metrics["f1"]),
            0.6894913912527211,
            delta=0.001,
        )
